# The ggplot2 phrasebook

ggplot2 proved that a grammar of graphics could be a working tool and not only a
theory. Most readers of this book already know it. gog follows the same grammar
and decides the details differently. This appendix covers both: which word to
write, and what behaves differently.

The translations assume gog can draw the plot you want. To find out whether it
can, read [Coverage](coverage.qmd). That appendix reads ggplot2's whole
reference index against the kernel, in both directions: what gog draws that
ggplot2 does not, and what ggplot2 draws that gog does not.

## Side by side

This first table compares the two systems as a whole, rather than word for word.

| | ggplot2 | gog |
|---|---|---|
| Languages | R | R, Python, Julia and JavaScript, all four calling one engine |
| Naming | `geom_point`, `aes`, `alpha` | `point`, channels by plain name, `opacity` |
| Where `x`/`y` are written | `aes()` at the plot or the layer, and a layer may override the plot's `aes()` | a mark takes every atom written after it, and none written before it |
| The histogram | `geom_histogram()` *or* `stat_bin(geom = "bar")` | `bar * bin` |
| Log axis | `scale_x_log10()` | `x(gdp, scale = "log")`, written on the binding |
| 3-D | external packages | one more position: `z` |
| Animation | gganimate, a separate package | `play` is a channel of the kernel: `+ play(year)` |

## Translations

This table is term for term. Find the ggplot2 call on the left, and the gog
sentence that draws the same plot is on the right.

| You write in ggplot2 | You write in gog |
|---|---|
| `ggplot(df, aes(x = a, y = b))` | `data(df) + x(a) + y(b) + …` |
| `geom_point()` | `point` |
| `geom_line()` | `line` |
| `geom_step()` | `step` |
| `geom_area()` | `area` |
| `geom_col()` | `bar` |
| `geom_bar()`, which counts the rows for you | `bar * count`, where the count is a word in the sentence |
| `geom_histogram(bins = 30)` | `bar * bin(30)` |
| `geom_freqpoly()` | `line * bin` |
| `geom_density()` | `line * density` |
| `geom_smooth()` | `line * smooth` |
| `stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "bar")` | `bar * mean` |
| `aes(color = g)` | `color(g)` |
| `aes(size = v)` | `size(v)` |
| `aes(shape = g)` | `shape(g)` |
| `aes(alpha = v)` | `opacity(v)` |
| `aes(group = g)` | `group(g)` |
| `scale_x_log10()` | `x(v, scale = "log")` |
| `scale_color_viridis_c()` | `color(v) + palette("viridis")` |
| `facet_grid(r ~ c)` | `\| facet(c) / facet(r)` |
| `facet_wrap(~ g, ncol = 4)` | `\| facet(g, wrap = 4)`. `/` runs the same line of panels down the page instead. The operator says the direction, so one number replaces both `nrow` and `ncol`. |
| `facet_*(scales = "free_y")` | `y(v, free = TRUE)`, written on the axis you are freeing. Nothing has to be chosen, because the binding already says which axis. |
| patchwork's <code>p1 &#124; p2</code>, `p1 / p2` | <code>plot_a &#124; plot_b</code>, `plot_a / plot_b`: the same two operators. What stands on the right decides the job: a plot composes, a `facet()` splits panels. |
| patchwork's `plot_spacer()`, `plot_layout(widths =)` | `theme(width =, height =)` on the plot that needs more room. No spacer is needed: both marginals stop where the main panel stops, and the corner is the room left over. |
| ggrepel's `geom_text_repel()` | `text * repel`, the collision modifier for overlapping labels, beside `dodge`, `stack` and `jitter` |
| ggExtra's `ggMarginal()` | <code>top / (main &#124; right)</code>, three ordinary plots ([Composition](composition.qmd)) |
| `coord_flip()` | swap the `x` and `y` bindings: orientation is read off whichever axis carries the categories, so there is nothing to switch |
| `labs(title = , x = , y = )` | `title()`, `x_label()`, `y_label()`, `z_label()` |
| `color = "red"`, `alpha = 0.5` inside a `geom_*()` | `style(color = "red", opacity = 0.5)` |
| `theme(…)` | `theme()` is the page, and there is one of it; `style()` belongs to one layer |
| `ggsave("plot.svg")` | the rendered plot *is* SVG; `render_svg()`, spelled the same way in all four languages, returns it as text you can write to a file |

## Six differences to expect

The words translate, but six things behave differently once they are in place.

- **`+` is still `+`, and on purpose.** ggplot2's author has said the pipe would
  have been the better interface [@wickham2018pipe]. gog kept `+` for two
  reasons. Python has no pipe operator of its own, so a pipe could not spell one
  syntax in all four languages. A pipe also makes every atom a function, and
  `bar * bin` has no meaning once both sides are functions.
  [Operators](operators.qmd) covers this in full, including which atoms commute
  in gog and did not commute in ggplot2.
- **Nothing is computed unless you name it.** `bar` draws your numbers
  unchanged. `geom_bar()` counts rows on its own, and gog counts only when you
  write `bar * count`.
- **There is one spelling.** No geom/stat pairs, and no choice of which function
  to use. If you can spell one plot two ways here, one of them is a bug.
  Report it as an issue on the book's repository.
- **The scale belongs to the binding.** You name a channel once, and its scale
  is a property of that binding. There is no second atom that names the channel
  again.
- **Setting is not mapping.** A constant maps no column, so it earns no legend.
  Write it in `style()`. In ggplot2 `aes(color = "red")` is legal and draws a
  legend with one entry called "red". Here `color("red")` asks for a column
  called `red`, so gog refuses it and names `style(color = "red")` as the fix.
- **Refusals name the fix.** A sentence gog cannot draw is refused, and the
  message names the sentence it would accept. Where you are used to a warning
  and a plot, gog stops and draws nothing. This book shows refusals on purpose:
  it runs the refused sentence and prints the message you would see.
